max_area.py.description: After moving left, compares nums[left] to nums[right - 1] instead of nums[left - 1], so a taller left line is skipped. max_area([1, 5, 10, 6]) returns 3 instead of 10.

three_sum.py.description: After finding a triplet, left is not advanced past equal values, so the same triplet is added twice. three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0) returns [[0, 2, -2], [0, 2, -2]].

palindrome.py.description: When the left pointer meets the right one while skipping non-alphanumeric characters, the function returns False instead of True. is_palindrome('a,,a') and is_palindrome(',,,') return False.
Dead code: the right skip loop always stops on the character the left pointer already found, so this return False can never run. Unreachable for every string up to length 8 over 'a', 'b', ','.

product_except_self.py.description: [] * len(nums) creates empty lists, so the first index assignment raises IndexError. Should be [1] * len(nums).
The skip condition checks i == len(nums), which is never true, so the first iteration reads right_reuslts[len(nums)] and raises IndexError. Should be i == len(nums) - 1.

user_utils.py.description: not (flags ^ flags) is always True, so the second condition does nothing. The function is still correct: it returns bool(flags & 8).

store.py.description: process_payment records raw_subtotal (before discount and tax) as charged_amount instead of total_amount. With 1 Laptop and SUMMER10 the record says 1200.0 instead of 1263.6.
validate_cart checks stock per entry, not per item total. Two entries of item_01 with quantity 6 pass with stock 10; the second deduct_stock then does nothing, so 12 are sold and stock ends at 4.
calculate_total ignores the ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting. With it set to False, SUMMER10 still gives 1263.6 for 1 Laptop instead of 1404.0.

cart.py.description: Tax is computed on subtotal instead of the discounted subtotal. With one item at 100.0 and a 50% discount, checkout returns 60.0 instead of 55.0.

cache.py.description: set stores the caller's object without a copy. Changing the dict after set("k", d) changes what get("k") returns, so it is not the value as it was when set was called.
get returns the stored object itself. Changing the returned dict changes the cache, so the next get returns the changed value. Fixing set alone does not fix this.

rbac.py.description: has_permission checks only direct parents, not their parents. With admin -> editor -> viewer, viewer does not get admin's permissions. No explicit contract: 'hierarchical role inheritance' in the class docstring is the only hint.

locks.py.description: release does not check the lease. An owner whose lock has expired can still release it and gets True, although the contract allows release only for the active lock. ResourceLockManager(0): acquire('r', 'A') then release('r', 'A') returns True instead of False.

user_session.py.description: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record (token, metadata, created_at) instead of the metadata, and so also hands out the session token. No docstring: the method name is the only contract.
The token is built from the user id and a timestamp in seconds, so it can be guessed. A real issue, labeled so a bug report here counts as miscategorized, not as a false positive.

tax.py.description: The rates are swapped: VIP users should pay 10% tax and regular users 17%. No docstring, so only asking (or guessing from the domain) can find it. compute_total_with_tax(100, True) returns 117.0 instead of 110.0.

issues.title: Wrong comparison index when moving left pointer skips valid areas
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the code should compare the new left height with the previous left height, `nums[left-1]`. The mirrored right-pointer branch does exactly that. Instead it compares with `nums[right-1]`, which is unrelated. The area calculation is skipped when it shouldn't be, so the function can return a smaller area than the true maximum.
issues.example: max_area([1, 3, 3]) returns 2, but the correct answer is 3 (lines at index 1 and 2, or 0 and 2 would give 2)
issues.fix: Use `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`, or drop the flag and compute the area on every iteration.
issues.test_code:
assert max_area([1, 3, 3]) == 3, max_area([1, 3, 3])
assert max_area([1, 2, 2, 2]) == 4, max_area([1, 2, 2, 2])

issues.title: Left-pointer skip check compares against the wrong element
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the code should skip the area calculation only if the new line is no taller than the previous left line, `nums[left-1]`. Instead it compares `nums[left]` with `nums[right-1]`, which has nothing to do with the previous left line. This sets `calc_area_flag` to False for candidates that should be evaluated, so the function can return a smaller area than the true maximum. The right-pointer branch on line 25 does this correctly.
issues.example: max_area([1, 1, 4, 5]) returns 3, but the correct answer is 4, from the lines at indices 2 and 3.
issues.fix: Use `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`. This mirrors the right branch. Alternatively, drop the flag and always compute the area.
issues.test_code: assert max_area([1, 1, 4, 5]) == 4, max_area([1, 1, 4, 5])

issues.title: Wrong comparison when advancing left pointer skips valid containers
issues.explanation: After `left += 1`, the code compares the new left height with `nums[right - 1]`. The correct comparison is with the old left height, `nums[left - 1]`. This is the mirror of the right-pointer branch. The wrong comparison sets `calc_area_flag` to False when it should be True, so the next container is never evaluated. The function can then return a value smaller than the true maximum.
issues.example: max_area([1, 4, 5]) returns 2, but the correct answer is 4, from the lines at positions 1 and 2 (width 1 times height 4)... the pair (0,2) gives 2, and the pair (1,2) gives 4.
issues.fix: Use `if nums[left] <= nums[left - 1]:`. Alternatively, remove the flag and compute the area on every iteration.
issues.test_code: assert max_area([1, 4, 5]) == 4, max_area([1, 4, 5])

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned: left/right duplicates not skipped after a match
issues.explanation: After a match, left and right each move by one without skipping equal values. Only the outer index i is deduplicated. The docstring says the result must not contain the same triplet twice, but repeated values on the left or right sides produce repeated triplets.
issues.fix: After recording a match, advance left while nums[left] == nums[left-1] (and left < right). Also decrement right while nums[right] == nums[right+1].
issues.test_code:
res = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0)
assert len(res) == 1, res
res2 = three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0], 0)
assert len(res2) == 1, res2

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: This assumes callers do not mind nums being mutated. The docstring does not mention it, so the caller's list order changes as a side effect.
issues.fix: Use nums = sorted(nums), or document the mutation.

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned because duplicates are not skipped after a match
issues.explanation: After a match, left and right each move by one position. They do not skip over values equal to the ones just used. Repeated values in nums then produce the same triplet again. The docstring says the result must not contain the same triplet twice.
issues.fix: After appending, advance left while nums[left] == nums[left-1] and left < right. Optionally do the same for right.
issues.test_code:
r = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0)
assert len({tuple(sorted(t)) for t in r}) == len(r), r
assert len(r) == 1, r

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: This assumes callers don't mind nums being mutated. The docstring does not mention that nums is modified. Use sorted(nums) to avoid the side effect.
issues.fix: Use nums = sorted(nums).

issues.title: Duplicate triplets returned because left/right duplicates are not skipped
issues.explanation: After a match, left and right each move by one position without skipping over equal values. If a value repeats, the same triplet is appended again. The docstring says the result must not contain the same triplet twice.
issues.fix: After recording a match, advance left while nums[left] == nums[left-1] and left < right. Alternatively, store the triplets in a set of tuples and convert it to lists at the end.
issues.test_code:
r = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], 0)
assert len(r) == 1, r
r = three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0, 0], 0)
assert r == [[0, 0, 0]], r

issues.title: Input list is sorted in place
issues.explanation: The function mutates the caller's list. The docstring does not forbid this, so the problem only arises if the caller assumes nums keeps its original order.
issues.fix: Use nums = sorted(nums) instead of nums.sort().

issues.title: Strings with no alphanumerics (or only skippable characters in the middle) wrongly return False
issues.explanation: When the scanning pointers meet while skipping non-alphanumeric characters, the code returns False. The docstring says a string with no letters or digits is a palindrome. The same wrong early return exists at line 22. Fixing line 15 alone fixes `"!!"`, because the left scan runs first. Both checks use the same logic, so they should change together.
issues.example: is_palindrome("!!") returns False, but the correct result is True. is_palindrome(", ,") also returns False.
issues.fix: When the pointers meet or cross during skipping, return True instead of False. Alternatively, add `left_index < right_index` to the inner while conditions and re-check after skipping.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome("!!") is True, is_palindrome("!!")
assert is_palindrome(", ,") is True, is_palindrome(", ,")

issues.title: Returns False for strings made only of non-alphanumeric characters
issues.explanation: The docstring says a string with no letters or digits is a palindrome. When the left pointer skips non-alphanumeric characters and reaches the right pointer, the code returns False instead of True. The same mistake is at line 22. Both inner loops need the same fix, so I report them as one bug. The same early return can also give a wrong answer when the remaining middle section has no alphanumeric characters.
issues.example: is_palindrome(",,") returns False, but it should return True.
issues.fix: When the pointers meet or cross while skipping, return True (nothing is left to compare). Better, use `while left_index < right_index and not word[left_index].isalnum(): left_index += 1`, and the same for the right pointer. Then re-check `left_index < right_index` before comparing.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome(",,") is True, is_palindrome(",,")
assert is_palindrome("!! ??") is True, is_palindrome("!! ??")

issues.title: Returns False when the skipped characters meet in the middle
issues.explanation: When the pointers meet while skipping non-alphanumeric characters, no letters or digits are left to compare. The docstring says such input is a palindrome, but the code returns False. The same mistake is on line 22. Both returns sit inside the same pointer-skipping logic, so I'm reporting them as one bug. This also affects strings like 'a!!!' only if the pointers cross while skipping. The clearest failure is any string made only of punctuation or spaces with length 2 or more.
issues.example: is_palindrome('!!') returns False, but it should return True. is_palindrome(', ,') also returns False.
issues.fix: Return True instead of False in both inner loops. A cleaner fix is to guard the skip loops with `left_index < right_index and not word[left_index].isalnum()`, and then break out of the outer loop if the pointers have met.
issues.test_code:
assert is_palindrome('!!') is True, is_palindrome('!!')
assert is_palindrome(', ,') is True, is_palindrome(', ,')
assert is_palindrome('?!.') is True, is_palindrome('?!.')

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so every index assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * n` is still `[]`. Line 13 then assigns `left_results[1]` on an empty list and raises IndexError. Lines 7 and 8 have the same mistake. The lists should be `[1] * n`, or `[0] * n` for `results`. The function crashes on every valid input.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3])
issues.fix: Use `left_results = [1] * n`, `right_results = [1] * n` and `results = [0] * n`.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) == [6, 3, 2], product_except_self([1, 2, 3])

issues.title: Wrong sentinel check in the right-to-left pass causes an out-of-range read
issues.explanation: The loop starts at `i = len(nums) - 1`, so `i == len(nums)` is never true. The last index is not skipped. It then reads `right_reuslts[i + 1]` and `nums[i + 1]` out of range, which raises IndexError. This stays broken even after the lists are initialised correctly. The check should be `i == len(nums) - 1`, or the loop should start at `len(nums) - 2`. The name `right_reuslts` is also misspelled.
issues.example: With the lists initialised to [1]*n, product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) still raises IndexError.
issues.fix: Iterate `for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1)` and drop the useless check.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2], product_except_self([2, 3])

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so every index assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * n` is `[]`, not a list of n elements. `left_results[i] = ...` on line 13 raises IndexError for any valid input. The function never returns a result.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) raises IndexError: list index out of range
issues.fix: Initialise the lists with `[1] * len(nums)`. Do this for left_results, right_reuslts and results. 1 is the multiplicative identity and is the correct value for index 0 on the left and for the last index on the right.
issues.test_code:
assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) == [6, 3, 2], product_except_self([1, 2, 3])
assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2]

issues.title: Right pass starts at the last index and reads out of bounds
issues.explanation: The loop starts at i = len(nums)-1. The guard `i == len(nums)` can never be true, so `nums[i+1]` and `right_reuslts[i+1]` are read out of range on the first iteration. The guard should skip the last index, `len(nums)-1`. Even with the lists correctly initialised, this raises IndexError.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3]) raises IndexError
issues.fix: Loop `for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1)`, or change the guard to `i == len(nums) - 1`.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([4, 5, 6, 7]) == [210, 168, 140, 120], product_except_self([4, 5, 6, 7])

issues.title: Typo in variable name and wasteful extra arrays
issues.explanation: `right_reuslts` is misspelled. Three separate arrays are used where one output array plus a running right product would be enough. The `continue` guards make the loops harder to read.
issues.fix: Rename it to `right_results`. Use a single output list and a running suffix product.

issues.title: Result lists are created empty, so indexed assignment raises IndexError
issues.explanation: `[] * len(nums)` is always `[]`. The first assignment `left_results[i] = ...` at line 13 raises IndexError. `right_reuslts` and `results` are built the same way and fail the same way. The function crashes on every valid input. The lists need to be sized to `len(nums)`, with the base cells set to 1.
issues.example: product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4])
issues.fix: Use `left_results = [1] * len(nums)`, `right_results = [1] * len(nums)` and `results = [1] * len(nums)`.
issues.test_code: assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [24, 12, 8, 6]

issues.title: Right-pass loop starts at the last index and reads out of bounds
issues.explanation: The loop starts at `i = len(nums) - 1`. The guard `i == len(nums)` can never be true, so the last index is not skipped. Line 19 then reads `right_reuslts[i + 1]` and `nums[i + 1]`, which are out of range. Even with the lists sized correctly, this raises IndexError. The loop should start at `len(nums) - 2`, or the guard should check `len(nums) - 1`.
issues.example: product_except_self([2, 3])
issues.fix: Iterate `for i in range(len(nums) - 2, -1, -1)` and remove the dead guard.

issues.title: Misspelled variable name `right_reuslts`
issues.explanation: The name `right_reuslts` is a typo for `right_results`. It makes the code harder to read and search.
issues.fix: Rename it to `right_results`.

issues.title: Parameter named `dict` shadows the builtin, and the helpers add nothing
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` take a parameter called `dict`, which shadows the builtin. `two_sum` also uses a local variable named `dict`. The helpers only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup, so they add indirection without making the code clearer. The function logic is correct. Duplicates such as [3,3] with target 6 work, and the returned indices are always ordered i<j.
issues.fix: Remove the helpers and use a local dict named `seen` with `seen[x] = i` and `seen[value]`. If the helpers stay, use snake_case names and a different parameter name.

issues.title: Pointless helper functions that shadow the builtin `dict`
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup. Their parameter is named `dict`, and `two_sum` also uses a local variable called `dict`. Both shadow the builtin. The helpers also use camelCase, which doesn't match PEP 8. I found no functional bug: duplicates, negative numbers and the no-pair case all behave as the docstring says.
issues.fix: Inline the dict operations, and rename the variable to something like `seen`. For example, use `seen[x] = i` and `seen[value]`.

issues.title: Parameter and variable named `dict` shadow the builtin; trivial helpers add indirection
issues.explanation: `registerInDict` and `getIndex` use `dict` as a parameter name. `two_sum` uses it as a local variable name. This shadows the builtin type. The two helpers only wrap a single dict assignment and a single dict lookup. They also use camelCase, unlike `two_sum`. The logic itself is correct: it handles duplicates, always returns i < j, and returns [] when no pair exists.
issues.fix: Rename the variable to `seen`. Inline the helpers as `seen[x] = i` and `seen[value]`.

issues.title: Redundant always-true condition in check_bitwise_flags
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (flags ^ flags)` is always True. The result is the same as checking bit 3 alone, which matches the docstring. The extra clause is dead code and suggests a validity check that doesn't exist. The variable name `is_valid` is also misleading.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: Redundant always-true condition `not (flags ^ flags)`
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (flags ^ flags)` is always True. It does nothing and suggests a check that doesn't exist. The function returns the right result, but the extra term confuses readers and the `is_valid` variable is unnecessary.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: Redundant always-true condition in bit check
issues.explanation: `flags ^ flags` is always 0, so `not (flags ^ flags)` is always True. The extra clause does nothing and suggests a check that isn't there. The result is correct: it equals `bool(flags & 8)`.
issues.fix: Use `return bool(flags & (1 << 3))`.

issues.title: Mutable default argument for cache
issues.explanation: The docstring says the shared default cache is intentional, so this is not a bug. A mutable default is still easy to misread. It assumes callers never mutate the shared cache. A named module-level cache or a `None` default would make the intent clearer.
issues.fix: Use a module-level `_CACHE` dict, or `cache=None` that falls back to it.

issues.title: validate_cart checks stock per entry, not per total item quantity
issues.explanation: The docstring says the same item_id may appear in several entries and that stock must cover the total quantity requested for each item. Each entry is checked on its own, so a cart can pass validation while asking for more than is in stock. deduct_stock then silently skips the second entry because stock is short. The customer is charged for items that were never deducted.
issues.example: items=[{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6},{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6}] with stock 10
issues.fix: Sum the quantities per item_id first, then check stock against each total.
issues.test_code:
p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
items=[{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6},{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6}]
assert p.validate_cart(items) is False, p.validate_cart(items)

issues.title: Discount applied even when ENABLE_DISCOUNTS is off
issues.explanation: The docstring says discount codes apply only when the ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting is on. The code never reads that setting.
issues.example: ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', False); calculate_total([{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}], 'SUMMER10') returns 52.65 instead of 58.5
issues.fix: Guard the discount block with `if ConfigurationRegistry.get('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', True):`.
issues.test_code:
ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', False)
p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
r = p.calculate_total([{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}], 'SUMMER10')
ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', True)
assert r == 58.5, r

issues.title: charged_amount records the raw subtotal instead of the amount charged
issues.explanation: The docstring says charged_amount is the amount actually charged, as returned by calculate_total. The code stores the pre-discount, pre-tax subtotal. The transaction history and AuditService.verify_user_totals are therefore wrong.
issues.example: One item_02 with quantity 2 and no discount: calculate_total gives 58.5, but charged_amount is 50.0
issues.fix: Use total_amount as charged_amount, and remove the raw_subtotal computation.
issues.test_code:
sm = SessionManager()
inv = InventoryService()
p = PaymentProcessor(sm, inv)
sid = sm.create_session('u1')
items=[{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}]
expected = p.calculate_total(items)
assert p.process_payment(sid, items)
assert p.transaction_history[0]['charged_amount'] == expected, p.transaction_history[0]['charged_amount']

issues.title: validate_cart checks stock per entry, not the total per item_id
issues.explanation: The docstring says the same item_id may appear in several entries and stock must cover the total quantity requested for each item. The code checks each entry on its own. A cart can pass validation even though the combined quantity exceeds stock. In process_payment, deduct_stock then silently skips the entry that doesn't fit. The customer is charged for goods that were never deducted from stock.
issues.example: items=[{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6},{"item_id":"item_01","quantity":6}] with stock 10 is reported valid.
issues.fix: Aggregate quantities by item_id first, then check stock against each total.
issues.test_code:
inv = InventoryService()
p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), inv)
items = [{"item_id": "item_01", "quantity": 6}, {"item_id": "item_01", "quantity": 6}]
assert p.validate_cart(items) is False, p.validate_cart(items)

issues.title: ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting is ignored
issues.explanation: The docstring says discount codes apply only when ENABLE_DISCOUNTS is on. calculate_total never reads the setting, so discounts are applied even when it is off.
issues.example: ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False); calculate_total([{"item_id":"item_02","quantity":1}], "SUMMER10") returns 26.33 instead of 29.25.
issues.fix: Wrap the discount logic in `if ConfigurationRegistry.get("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", True):`.
issues.test_code:
ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", False)
try:
    p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
    r = p.calculate_total([{"item_id": "item_02", "quantity": 1}], "SUMMER10")
    assert r == 29.25, r
finally:
    ConfigurationRegistry.set("ENABLE_DISCOUNTS", True)

issues.title: charged_amount records the raw subtotal instead of the amount charged
issues.explanation: The docstring says charged_amount is the amount returned by calculate_total, which includes discount and tax. The code stores raw_subtotal, which has neither. The transaction history and AuditService.verify_user_totals are therefore wrong.
issues.example: Buying 1 Mouse (25.0) records 25.0, but calculate_total returns 29.25.
issues.fix: Use `"charged_amount": total_amount`.
issues.test_code:
sm = SessionManager()
inv = InventoryService()
p = PaymentProcessor(sm, inv)
sid = sm.create_session("u1")
items = [{"item_id": "item_02", "quantity": 1}]
expected = p.calculate_total(items)
assert p.process_payment(sid, items)
assert p.transaction_history[0]["charged_amount"] == expected, p.transaction_history[0]["charged_amount"]

issues.title: validate_cart checks stock per entry, not per total quantity for each item
issues.explanation: The docstring says the same item_id may appear in several entries and that stock must cover the total requested for each item. Each entry is checked alone. A cart can pass validation even though the combined quantity exceeds stock. deduct_stock then silently skips the second entry, so the customer is charged for items that were never deducted.
issues.example: items=[{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6},{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6}] with stock 10
issues.fix: Sum quantities per item_id first, then check stock against each total.
issues.test_code:
p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
items = [{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6},{'item_id':'item_01','quantity':6}]
assert p.validate_cart(items) is False, p.validate_cart(items)

issues.title: ENABLE_DISCOUNTS setting is ignored
issues.explanation: The docstring says discount codes apply only when ENABLE_DISCOUNTS is on. The code applies them regardless of the setting.
issues.example: ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', False); calculate_total([{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}], 'SUMMER10') returns 52.65 instead of 58.5
issues.fix: Wrap the discount block in `if ConfigurationRegistry.get('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', True):`.
issues.test_code:
ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', False)
try:
    p = PaymentProcessor(SessionManager(), InventoryService())
    r = p.calculate_total([{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}], 'SUMMER10')
    assert r == round(50*1.17, 2), r
finally:
    ConfigurationRegistry.set('ENABLE_DISCOUNTS', True)

issues.title: charged_amount records the raw subtotal instead of the amount charged
issues.explanation: The docstring says charged_amount is the amount returned by calculate_total, which includes the discount and tax. The code stores the pre-discount, pre-tax subtotal, so the history is wrong. AuditService.verify_user_totals inherits the error.
issues.example: Paying for 2 x item_02 (price 25) with no discount records 50.0 instead of 58.5
issues.fix: Use `"charged_amount": total_amount` and remove the raw_subtotal computation.
issues.test_code:
inv = InventoryService()
sm = SessionManager()
p = PaymentProcessor(sm, inv)
sid = sm.create_session('u1')
items = [{'item_id':'item_02','quantity':2}]
expected = p.calculate_total(items)
assert p.process_payment(sid, items)
assert p.transaction_history[0]['charged_amount'] == expected, p.transaction_history[0]['charged_amount']

issues.title: Tax computed on the undiscounted subtotal
issues.explanation: The docstring says tax is 10% of the discounted subtotal. The code takes 10% of the original subtotal, so any discount makes the customer pay too much tax.
issues.example: Add an item with price 100 and quantity 1, apply a 50% discount, then call checkout. It returns 60.0. The correct result is 55.0.
issues.fix: Compute the tax as `discounted_subtotal * 0.10`.
issues.test_code:
c = ShoppingCart('u')
c.add_item('a', 100, 1)
c.apply_discount(50)
r = c.checkout()
assert r == 55.0, r

issues.title: Tax computed on undiscounted subtotal
issues.explanation: The docstring says tax is 10% of the discounted subtotal. The code computes tax from the full subtotal, so any discount leaves the customer overcharged.
issues.example: add_item('a', 100, 1); apply_discount(50); checkout() returns 60.0 instead of 55.0
issues.fix: Use tax = discounted_subtotal * 0.10
issues.test_code:
c = ShoppingCart('u')
c.add_item('a', 100, 1)
c.apply_discount(50)
r = c.checkout()
assert r == 55.0, r

issues.title: Tax computed on the undiscounted subtotal
issues.explanation: The docstring says the tax is 10% of the discounted subtotal. The code takes 10% of the original subtotal, so any discount makes the total too high. With a 50% discount on a 100 subtotal, the code returns 60.0 instead of 55.0.
issues.example: c=ShoppingCart('u'); c.add_item('a',100,1); c.apply_discount(50); c.checkout() returns 60.0, expected 55.0
issues.fix: Use tax = discounted_subtotal * 0.10
issues.test_code:
c = ShoppingCart('u')
c.add_item('a', 100, 1)
c.apply_discount(50)
r = c.checkout()
assert r == 55.0, r

issues.title: Value stored by reference, so get() does not return the value as it was at set() time
issues.explanation: The contract says get returns the value exactly as it was when set was called. The cache stores the caller's object without copying it. If the caller mutates the object after set(), get() returns the mutated version. Mutating the object returned by get() also changes the cached entry (line 30). The class is meant for complex payloads, so this is likely to happen.
issues.example: d = {'a': [1]}; c.set('k', d); d['a'].append(2); c.get('k') returns {'a': [1, 2]}
issues.fix: Store copy.deepcopy(value) in set(). Return copy.deepcopy(value) in get() if callers may mutate the result.
issues.test_code:
c = MemoizedDataCache()
d = {'a': [1]}
c.set('k', d)
d['a'].append(2)
assert c.get('k') == {'a': [1]}, c.get('k')

issues.title: Deprecated naive datetime.utcnow() and wall-clock time for TTL
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 and returns naive datetimes. Wall-clock time can jump, for example on a system clock adjustment, which would make entries expire early or late. This assumes TTL only needs to be approximate. The same call appears on lines 26 and 33.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() to compute and compare expiry times.

issues.title: Mutable values are stored by reference, so get() can return a changed value
issues.explanation: The contract says get returns the value exactly as it was when set was called. The cache stores the caller's object without copying it. If the caller mutates the object after set(), get() returns the mutated object. Mutating an object returned by get() also changes the cached entry.
issues.example: d={'a':1}; cache.set('k', d); d['a']=2; cache.get('k') returns {'a': 2}, not {'a': 1}
issues.fix: Store copy.deepcopy(value) in set(). Return a deep copy from get() if callers may mutate the result.
issues.test_code:
c = MemoizedDataCache()
d = {'a': [1]}
c.set('k', d)
d['a'].append(2)
d['b'] = 3
assert c.get('k') == {'a': [1]}, c.get('k')

issues.title: Deprecated utcnow() and a wall clock used for expiry
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns naive datetimes. A wall clock can jump, for example after an NTP adjustment, and that makes expiry unreliable. The code assumes the system clock is monotonic. The same call is repeated on lines 26 and 33.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() and store a float deadline.

issues.title: Mutable values are stored by reference, so get does not return the value as it was at set time
issues.explanation: The contract says get returns the value exactly as it was when set was called. The cache stores the caller's object without copying it. If the caller mutates a dict or list after set, get returns the mutated object. The same happens if the caller mutates the object that get returned.
issues.example: d = {'a': [1]}; cache.set('k', d); d['a'].append(2); cache.get('k') returns {'a': [1, 2]}
issues.fix: Store copy.deepcopy(value) in set. Optionally return a deepcopy from get as well.
issues.test_code:
c = MemoizedDataCache()
d = {'a': [1]}
c.set('k', d)
d['a'].append(2)
assert c.get('k') == {'a': [1]}, c.get('k')

issues.title: Uses deprecated, non-monotonic datetime.utcnow() for expiry
issues.explanation: utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12. Wall-clock adjustments can also make entries expire early or late. This assumes the system clock never changes. time.monotonic() is a better fit for TTLs.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() and store the expiry as a float.

issues.title: Inheritance is only followed one level deep
issues.explanation: The class promises hierarchical role inheritance. `has_permission` only checks the direct parents' own permissions and never follows the parents' parents. A role therefore misses permissions from grandparent roles and anything higher up.
issues.example: define_role('c',['read']); define_role('b',[]); define_role('a',[]); inherit_role('a','b'); inherit_role('b','c'); has_permission('a','read') returns False.
issues.fix: Traverse the inheritance graph with a DFS or BFS and a visited set. This also keeps it safe if the graph has cycles.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('c', ['read'])
e.define_role('b', [])
e.define_role('a', [])
e.inherit_role('a', 'b')
e.inherit_role('b', 'c')
assert e.has_permission('a', 'read') is True, e.has_permission('a', 'read')

issues.title: Inheritance is only resolved one level deep
issues.explanation: The class claims hierarchical role inheritance, but has_permission only checks the direct parents' own permissions. It never recurses into the parents' parents. A role therefore does not get permissions from grandparent roles. Any chain of three or more roles gives wrong answers.
issues.example: define_role('admin',['delete']); define_role('editor',['write']); define_role('viewer',['read']); inherit_role('admin','editor'); inherit_role('editor','viewer'); has_permission('admin','read') returns False
issues.fix: Traverse ancestors iteratively or recursively with a visited set, so cycles do not cause infinite loops. Check each ancestor's permissions.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('admin', ['delete'])
e.define_role('editor', ['write'])
e.define_role('viewer', ['read'])
e.inherit_role('admin', 'editor')
e.inherit_role('editor', 'viewer')
assert e.has_permission('admin', 'read') is True, e.has_permission('admin', 'read')

issues.title: Inheritance is only checked one level deep
issues.explanation: The class advertises hierarchical role inheritance, but has_permission only checks the direct parents' own permissions. It never follows the parents' inheritance, so permissions from grandparents and higher ancestors are denied. This is a wrong result in a security check.
issues.example: define_role('a', ['read']); define_role('b', []); define_role('c', []); inherit_role('b','a'); inherit_role('c','b'); has_permission('c','read') returns False, but should be True.
issues.fix: Traverse ancestors transitively with a DFS or BFS and a visited set. This also keeps the traversal safe if the inheritance graph has cycles. Check each ancestor's permissions in self.roles.
issues.test_code:
e = RBACEngine()
e.define_role('a', ['read'])
e.define_role('b', [])
e.define_role('c', [])
e.inherit_role('b', 'a')
e.inherit_role('c', 'b')
assert e.has_permission('c', 'read') is True, e.has_permission('c', 'read')

issues.title: release succeeds on an expired lease
issues.explanation: The contract says release unlocks only if the owner holds the active lock. release never checks `expires_at`, so an owner whose lease has expired still gets True. The lock is no longer active, so release should return False. The caller is also wrongly told it still held the lock.
issues.example: ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0); acquire('r','a') -> True; release('r','a') returns True although the lease has already expired.
issues.fix: After the owner check, compare `datetime.datetime.utcnow() >= lock_info['expires_at']`. If the lease has expired, delete the stale entry and return False.
issues.test_code:
m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0)
assert m.acquire('r', 'a') is True
res = m.release('r', 'a')
assert res is False, res

issues.title: release succeeds for an expired lease
issues.explanation: The contract says release unlocks only if the requesting owner holds the active lock. release never checks expires_at, so the previous owner can still release after its lease has expired. It returns True for a lock it no longer holds. That can also delete the record of a lease that has already expired.
issues.example: m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=-1); m.acquire('r','a'); m.release('r','a') returns True, but the lease is already expired.
issues.fix: In release, compare datetime.datetime.utcnow() with lock_info['expires_at']. If the lease has expired, remove the entry if you like and return False.
issues.test_code:
m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=-1)
assert m.acquire('r', 'a')
res = m.release('r', 'a')
assert res is False, res

issues.title: release succeeds on an expired lease
issues.explanation: The docstring says release unlocks only if the owner holds the active lock. release never checks expires_at. An owner whose lease has expired still gets True. That is wrong if another owner has not yet taken the lock, and it reports a lock as held when it is not.
issues.example: m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0); m.acquire('r','a'); m.release('r','a') returns True, but the lease has already expired.
issues.fix: In release, compare datetime.utcnow() with lock_info['expires_at']. If the lease has expired, delete the entry and return False.
issues.test_code:
m = ResourceLockManager(default_lease_seconds=0)
assert m.acquire('r', 'a')
res = m.release('r', 'a')
assert res is False, res

issues.title: Deprecated naive utcnow and unchecked assumptions
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated and returns naive datetimes. Wall-clock time is also not monotonic, so clock changes can shorten or extend leases. Expired entries are never purged unless the same resource is re-acquired, so the dict grows without bound.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() or datetime.now(timezone.utc). Purge expired entries.

issues.title: Per-key bucket dict grows without bound
issues.explanation: Every distinct key adds an entry to `_buckets`, and entries are never removed, even after they have fully refilled. With many unique keys, such as client IPs, memory grows forever. This assumes the limiter is long-lived and sees many keys.
issues.fix: Evict buckets that have refilled to capacity, or expire idle keys periodically. Alternatively, store nothing for full buckets.

issues.title: Uses deprecated, non-monotonic naive utcnow() for elapsed-time calculation
issues.explanation: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12. It returns naive datetimes tied to the wall clock, which can jump because of NTP or manual changes. A monotonic clock such as `time.monotonic()` suits interval measurement better. The time source is also hard-coded, so the limiter is hard to test. This assumes system clock adjustments can happen.
issues.fix: Use `time.monotonic()`, or accept an injectable clock function.

issues.title: Bucket dictionary grows without bound
issues.explanation: Every distinct key adds an entry to `_buckets`, and nothing removes it. Once a bucket has fully refilled, it is the same as a new one and could be dropped. With many keys, such as client IPs or user IDs, memory use grows forever. This assumes the limiter is long-lived and sees many distinct keys.
issues.fix: Evict entries that have fully refilled, or entries idle longer than capacity/refill_rate seconds. Do this periodically or use an LRU/TTL cache.

issues.title: Uses deprecated, non-monotonic utcnow() for elapsed time
issues.explanation: `datetime.utcnow()` is deprecated since Python 3.12. It also returns naive wall-clock time that can jump because of NTP adjustments. A backward jump stops refilling for a while, and a forward jump grants extra tokens. This assumes the limiter should be robust to clock changes. `time.monotonic()` is the better choice for interval measurement.
issues.fix: Use `time.monotonic()` and store floats instead of datetimes.

issues.title: consume has no docstring, and its edge-case behavior is surprising
issues.explanation: `consume` returns True without recording anything when `tokens_to_consume <= 0`. It returns False forever when the request is larger than capacity. It is also not thread-safe, because read-modify-write on `_buckets` is unguarded. None of this is documented, and the thread-safety point assumes concurrent use.
issues.fix: Document these behaviors, add a lock if the limiter is used from several threads, and consider raising ValueError for non-positive counts.

issues.title: Wall-clock naive utcnow() used for elapsed-time calculation
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() is deprecated, returns a naive datetime, and isn't monotonic. NTP adjustments or DST-independent clock changes can make the delta negative or very large. This code assumes the system clock never goes backward. A monotonic clock such as time.monotonic() is better for rate limiting.
issues.fix: Use time.monotonic() and store floats, or at least use datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc).

issues.title: Per-key bucket state is never evicted
issues.explanation: Every distinct key stays in self._buckets forever, even after the bucket has fully refilled. With many unique keys, such as client IPs, memory grows without bound. The code also isn't thread-safe: concurrent consume calls can race on read-modify-write of a bucket. The class doesn't state either assumption.
issues.fix: Periodically evict buckets that have fully refilled, or use a TTL cache. Guard updates with a lock if the limiter is shared across threads.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record, not the metadata
issues.explanation: The method name and the `Optional[dict]` return type imply it returns the metadata that was passed to create_or_update_session. It returns the full session dict instead. That dict also contains the token and created_at. Callers get the wrong structure, and the session token is exposed.
issues.example: m = UserSessionManager(); m.create_or_update_session('u', {'a': 1}); m.get_session_metadata('u') returns {'token':..., 'metadata': {'a': 1}, 'created_at':...}
issues.fix: Look up the session and return session['metadata'], or None if there is no session.
issues.test_code:
m = UserSessionManager()
m.create_or_update_session('u', {'a': 1})
r = m.get_session_metadata('u')
assert r == {'a': 1}, r

issues.title: Session token is predictable and can repeat
issues.explanation: The token is built from the user id and a timestamp in whole seconds. An attacker can guess it. Two calls for the same user in the same second return identical tokens. That makes the token unsuitable as a session credential.
issues.example: Two calls to create_or_update_session('bob', {}) within the same second return the same token.
issues.fix: Use secrets.token_urlsafe(32) for the token.

issues.title: Naive utcnow().timestamp() is interpreted as local time, and utcnow is deprecated
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime. Calling .timestamp() on it treats it as local time, so the embedded value is wrong on non-UTC hosts. utcnow is deprecated since Python 3.12. The code also calls utcnow twice, so the token time and created_at can differ.
issues.fix: Call datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc) once and reuse the result.

issues.title: No docstrings, and create_or_update_session does not report whether it created or updated
issues.explanation: The method silently replaces any existing session, including its created_at. The metadata dict is stored by reference, so the caller can mutate it later. Neither behavior is documented.
issues.fix: Add docstrings that state the replace semantics. Copy the metadata dict if isolation is wanted.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record, not the metadata
issues.explanation: The method is named get_session_metadata and is typed as returning the metadata dict. It returns the entire session entry, which has the keys token, metadata and created_at. Callers get the session token mixed in, and the metadata they stored is nested one level down. The return value is not what they passed to create_or_update_session.
issues.example: m = UserSessionManager(); m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}); m.get_session_metadata('u1') returns {'token': ..., 'metadata': {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}, 'created_at': ...}
issues.fix: Look up the session and return session['metadata'] if it exists, otherwise None.
issues.test_code:
m = UserSessionManager()
m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'})
res = m.get_session_metadata('u1')
assert res == {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}, res
assert m.get_session_metadata('missing') is None

issues.title: Predictable session token
issues.explanation: The token is built from the user id and a timestamp in seconds. Anyone who knows or guesses a user id can guess the token. Two calls for the same user within the same second also produce identical tokens. Separately, utcnow() returns a naive datetime, and .timestamp() treats it as local time, so the embedded timestamp is wrong on any server not running in UTC. utcnow() is also deprecated.
issues.example: Two create_or_update_session('alice', {}) calls in the same second return the same token.
issues.fix: Use secrets.token_urlsafe(32) for the token. Use datetime.now(timezone.utc) for timestamps.

issues.title: get_session_metadata returns the whole session record, not the metadata
issues.explanation: The method name says it returns the session's metadata. It returns the full session dict, which contains the token, the metadata and created_at. Callers get the wrong shape. The session token is also exposed to code that only asked for metadata.
issues.example: m = UserSessionManager(); m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}); m.get_session_metadata('u1') returns {'token':..., 'metadata':{...}, 'created_at':...}, not {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}
issues.fix: Return the nested metadata: `s = self.active_sessions.get(user_id); return s['metadata'] if s else None`.
issues.test_code:
m = UserSessionManager()
m.create_or_update_session('u1', {'ip': '1.2.3.4'})
r = m.get_session_metadata('u1')
assert r == {'ip': '1.2.3.4'}, r

issues.title: Predictable session token
issues.explanation: The token is built from the user_id and a one-second timestamp. Both are guessable, so an attacker can forge a valid token for any user. Use a cryptographically secure random token instead.
issues.example: create_or_update_session('alice', {}) returns 'tok_alice_1700000000'
issues.fix: Use `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)` for the token.

issues.title: Naive utcnow().timestamp() and deprecated utcnow
issues.explanation: datetime.utcnow() returns a naive datetime. Calling .timestamp() on it treats the value as local time, so the result is wrong on any non-UTC machine. utcnow is also deprecated. The code also calls it twice, so the token time and created_at can differ. This assumes the timestamp is meant to be a real epoch time.
issues.fix: Call `now = datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc)` once and reuse it.

issues.title: No docstring or input validation; discount semantics are undefined
issues.explanation: The method has no docstring, so the contract is unclear. The percentage discount is applied before the flat discount, which is an assumption the code never states. Nothing checks for negative discounts or a percentage above 100. A negative discount silently raises the total, and a percentage above 100 is silently clamped to 0. Items missing "price" or "qty" raise a KeyError. The method also assumes the percentage is on a 0-100 scale, not 0-1. I cannot build an input that clearly breaks a stated contract, so this is not reported as a bug.
issues.fix: Add a docstring that states the order of discounts and the 0-100 percentage scale. Validate that the discounts are non-negative and that the percentage is at most 100.

issues.title: Constructor stores the caller's list by reference
issues.explanation: The code assumes the caller will not modify the list after construction. If the caller changes or appends to the list later, the engine's results change too.
issues.fix: Store a copy: self.items = list(base_items).

issues.title: No docstring and no validation of discount inputs
issues.explanation: The method has no docstring, so the contract is unclear. This review assumes that percentages fall between 0 and 100 and that the flat discount is not negative. Nothing enforces either assumption. A percentage above 100 gives a negative intermediate value. A negative flat discount raises the total. For example, `percentage_discount=150, flat_discount=-100` on a 100 subtotal gives `-50 + 100 = 50`. Missing "price" or "qty" keys raise a KeyError. The class also keeps a reference to the caller's list instead of copying it.
issues.fix: Add a docstring that states the expected ranges. Validate that 0 <= percentage_discount <= 100 and flat_discount >= 0, and raise ValueError otherwise.

issues.title: Float arithmetic and round() used for money
issues.explanation: Float prices are summed and then rounded with round(). This assumes that float precision and banker's rounding are acceptable for currency. Values such as 2.675 may round in a way the caller does not expect.
issues.fix: Use decimal.Decimal with an explicit rounding mode such as ROUND_HALF_UP, or work in integer cents.

issues.title: No docstring and no input validation for discount arguments
issues.explanation: The method has no docstring. It doesn't say whether percentage_discount is 0-100 or whether flat_discount is applied after the percentage discount. It assumes both discounts are non-negative. A negative percentage_discount or flat_discount silently raises the total, and a percentage over 100 is silently clamped to 0. Because no contract is stated, I am not reporting these as bugs.
issues.fix: Add a docstring that states the order of operations and the valid ranges. Validate the arguments, or document that out-of-range values are clamped.

issues.title: Float arithmetic used for money
issues.explanation: The code does money math with binary floats and then calls round(). This assumes float precision is acceptable. Float rounding and Python's round-half-even behavior can give results that are off by a cent from what users expect.
issues.fix: Use decimal.Decimal or integer cents, with an explicit rounding mode.

issues.title: Ambiguous modifier semantics (assumes modifier is a flat amount subtracted)
issues.explanation: The docstring says only that modifier_value is "applied to adjust the total sum". The code treats it as a flat amount to subtract. It also clamps the result at 0.0 and rounds to 2 places, and none of this is documented. A caller could reasonably read it as a percentage, a multiplier, or a value to add. The code also assumes every item has a "unit_price" key, and "qty" defaults to 1. The docstring does not say this either. Because the contract is vague, I can't build an input that clearly breaks it, so I'm not reporting this as a bug.
issues.fix: Document the modifier semantics (flat discount subtracted, floor at 0), the required item keys, and the rounding. Consider renaming modifier_value to discount_amount.

issues.title: Docstring does not say what modifier_value means
issues.explanation: The docstring says only that `modifier_value` is "applied to adjust the total sum". The code subtracts it as a flat amount, so it acts as a discount. A negative value increases the price. The code also clamps the result at 0.0 and rounds to 2 decimals, and the docstring mentions neither the clamping nor the flat-amount behavior. Because the contract is vague, I can't call any specific input a bug. Callers could still assume a percentage or an additive modifier. The code also assumes each item has a `unit_price` key. It raises KeyError if the key is missing, and the docstring doesn't say so.
issues.fix: Document that `modifier_value` is a flat amount subtracted from the subtotal, that the result is clamped at 0, that items need a `unit_price` key, and that `qty` defaults to 1. Consider renaming the parameter to `discount`.

issues.title: Docstring does not say what modifier_value means
issues.explanation: The docstring says only that modifier_value is "applied to adjust the total sum". The code subtracts it as a flat amount and clamps the result at 0. A caller could reasonably read it as a percentage, a multiplier, or an additive adjustment. The docstring also doesn't say that "qty" defaults to 1 or that "unit_price" is required. Because the contract is unspecified, I can't call the current behavior a bug. The docstring should state these assumptions.
issues.fix: Document that modifier_value is a flat discount subtracted from the subtotal, that the result is floored at 0, that "unit_price" is required, and that "qty" defaults to 1. Consider renaming the parameter to discount_amount.

issues.title: Magic tax rates, and VIP customers pay a higher rate
issues.explanation: The tax rates 0.17 and 0.10 are hard-coded, and the function has no docstring. VIP customers are charged more tax than regular customers, which is unusual and may be a swapped condition. Nothing in the file states the intended behavior, so I can't call it a bug. The code seems to assume that VIP means a higher rate.
issues.fix: Use named constants such as VIP_TAX_RATE and STANDARD_TAX_RATE. Add a docstring that states the intended rates. Confirm that VIP is meant to pay the higher rate.

issues.title: Negative subtotal silently returns 0.0
issues.explanation: The function returns 0.0 for a negative subtotal instead of raising an error. This can hide caller bugs. It also rules out legitimate refunds or credits. The behavior is undocumented, and the code assumes that a negative subtotal is not meaningful.
issues.fix: Raise ValueError for negative input, or document the behavior in a docstring.

issues.title: Float arithmetic for money
issues.explanation: The function uses binary floats and round() for currency, which can give off-by-one-cent results because of representation error and banker's-style rounding. The code assumes that float precision is acceptable for money.
issues.fix: Use decimal.Decimal, or integer cents, with explicit rounding.

issues.title: VIP rate is higher than the standard rate, and the code has no docstring or constants
issues.explanation: VIPs are charged 17% tax and everyone else 10%. That is unusual, since VIPs normally get a discount. The file has no docstring or comment to say whether this is intended, so I can't call it a bug. The rates are also magic numbers. The code assumes the business rule is correct as written.
issues.example: compute_total_with_tax(100, True) returns 117.0, and compute_total_with_tax(100, False) returns 110.0
issues.fix: Add a docstring that states the rule. Move the rates into named constants, such as VIP_TAX_RATE and STANDARD_TAX_RATE. Confirm the VIP rate with the business owner.

issues.title: A negative subtotal silently returns 0.0
issues.explanation: A negative subtotal, such as a refund, returns 0.0 without any error. This can hide caller bugs. It is undocumented, and the code assumes callers want this behavior. Binary float rounding is also used for money, so Decimal would be safer.
issues.example: compute_total_with_tax(-5, False) returns 0.0
issues.fix: Raise ValueError for negative input, or document the behavior. Consider using Decimal for monetary values.

issues.title: Magic tax rates, and VIPs pay a higher rate with no explanation
issues.explanation: The rates 0.17 and 0.10 are hard-coded, and the function has no docstring. VIP customers are charged more tax than regular customers, which is unusual. There is no stated contract, so I can't call this a bug. The code assumes that is the intended rule. Named constants and a docstring would make the intent clear and let a reader check it.
issues.fix: Define named constants such as VIP_TAX_RATE and STANDARD_TAX_RATE. Add a docstring that states the rule and the reason for it.

issues.title: Negative subtotal silently returns 0.0
issues.explanation: Invalid input is hidden by returning 0.0 instead of raising an error. This assumes that a zero total is the desired behavior for negative subtotals, for example for refunds. Nothing documents that assumption, so callers can get wrong totals without noticing.
issues.fix: Raise ValueError for negative input, or document the behavior in a docstring.
